notes.meaning: Job is introduced as a godly man living in the land of Uz. He was blameless and upright, meaning he lived with sincere honesty and integrity before others rather than being completely sinless. His deep awe and reverence for God caused him to turn away from every kind of evil.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars highlight that Job was not an Israelite, but a Gentile living in Uz, a land likely located in or near Edom.

notes.meaning: God blessed Job with a large family of seven sons and three daughters. In the ancient world, having many children was seen as a special mark of God's kindness and favor. His house was filled with life and joy.

Job owned massive herds of livestock and employed a large number of workers to manage his estates. His great wealth and upright character made him the most influential man in the entire eastern region. He used his high standing and wealth to honor God and care for people in need.

Job's grown sons held regular dinners in their homes and invited their three sisters to join them. These gatherings showed the strong love, peace, and unity shared among the brothers and sisters. They enjoyed their blessings together without bitterness or rivalry.

When the days of feasting finished, Job gathered his children to help them prepare their hearts before God. Early in the morning, he offered burnt offerings for each of them, acting as the priest of his household. He worried that in their merrymaking they might have entertained careless or sinful thoughts toward God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translation translated the phrase about cursing God as having blessed God, using a literal rendering of the Hebrew wording.

notes.meaning: The scene moves to heaven, where angels called the sons of God came to report before the Lord. Satan entered the gathering among them as an uninvited enemy. Even though Satan opposes God, he is still a created being who must answer to the Almighty and cannot act without permission.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the Hebrew text refers to this figure as the satan or the accuser, functioning like a prosecuting officer in God's heavenly court rather than the devil of later Christian teaching.

notes.meaning: The Lord questioned Satan about where he had been, showing that the adversary is always held accountable to God. Satan answered that he had been roaming back and forth across the earth. This reveals how actively the enemy searches for opportunities to cause trouble and tempt people to fall.

The Lord pointed Satan's attention to Job, celebrating him as a servant without equal on earth. God openly praised Job's blameless character, his upright heart, and his faithful reverence that turned away from evil. God was honored by Job's genuine love and obedience.

Satan responded with a sneer, asking whether Job served God for nothing. He claimed that Job was only religious because of the personal benefits he received. The accuser refused to believe that anyone could love God simply for who He is.

Satan complained that God had placed a protective wall or hedge around Job, his family, and all his property. God had richly blessed Job's daily work and allowed his flocks to spread across the land. Satan argued that Job only stayed faithful because God made his life completely safe and comfortable.

Satan dared God to take away all of Job's wealth and blessings. He insisted that if Job lost his comforts, he would openly curse God to His face. The enemy wanted to prove that Job's godliness was shallow and driven entirely by money.

The Lord allowed Satan to test Job by striking his possessions, but placed a strict limit forbidding him from harming Job's body. God remained in complete control, setting the exact boundaries for the enemy's attack. Satan then left God's presence, eager to begin his destructive work.

Trouble began on a day when Job's children were gathered for a meal at their oldest brother's home. Satan selected a day of great peace and celebration to unleash his attack. This made the sudden wave of losses even more shocking and painful.

A messenger suddenly arrived while Job was at home to deliver tragic news. He reported that the oxen were plowing in the fields while the donkeys grazed peacefully nearby. This showed that the tragedy arrived during normal, honest daily work without any carelessness on the servants' part.

The messenger explained that Sabean raiders suddenly swooped down and carried off the animals. The bandits killed all the workers with swords, leaving only this one servant alive to tell Job the news. Satan intentionally spared a single survivor so Job would hear the painful report right away.

Before the first messenger could finish, a second ran up with more terrible news. He announced that the fire of God, meaning violent lightning, fell from heaven and wiped out the sheep and their keepers. This stroke was designed to make Job feel that God Himself had turned against him.

While that man was still reporting, a third runner arrived with another disaster. He told Job that Chaldean invaders formed three raiding parties, stole all the camels, and slaughtered the servants. In just moments, all of Job's livelihood was completely gone.

A fourth messenger came running while the previous one was still speaking. He brought news about Job's sons and daughters, who were eating together at their oldest brother's house. This led up to the most heartbreaking news Job could ever receive.

The messenger reported that a sudden desert whirlwind slammed into the house, causing the building to collapse and kill all ten children. Job lost all his precious sons and daughters in a single instant. Satan saved this crushing grief for the end, hoping it would finally break Job's faith.

Job stood up, tore his clothes, and shaved his head, using customary ancient actions to express agonizing sorrow. Rather than lashing out in rage or despair, he fell to the earth and worshiped God. He felt the sharpness of his grief deeply, yet chose to humble himself before his Creator.

Job acknowledged that he came into the world with nothing and would leave it with nothing. He confessed that every blessing came as a gift from the Lord, who had every right to withdraw what was His. Instead of cursing God as the devil expected, Job openly blessed the Lord's holy name.

differ.view: Many Baptists teach that God is completely sovereign over all events, so Job rightly saw God as the ultimate cause behind his losses rather than blaming chance or only the devil.

Some evangelicals emphasize that God only permits suffering rather than authoring it directly, noting that Satan was the active power behind the destruction while God allowed it for a greater purpose.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some prosperity teachers claim that God only gives and never takes away, arguing that Job spoke mistakenly in this verse and opened the door to trouble by making a negative statement.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate and the ancient Greek translation add an extra phrase to this verse: as it pleased the Lord, so is it done.

notes.meaning: Through all these crushing tragedies, Job remained faithful and did not commit sin with his lips or his heart. He refused to accuse God of doing anything wrong, foolish, or unfair. His steadfast trust proved that Satan's accusations against him were totally false.
